title: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning: LoRA, QLoRA, and the Deployment Contract
summary: Choose when to change model behavior, derive low-rank updates and memory budgets, and carry an adapter safely from supervised examples to an evaluated serving artifact.
learningObjectives: Distinguish knowledge retrieval from behavioral adaptation.
Calculate LoRA parameter counts and explain rank and scaling.
Separate quantized storage, compute precision, and optimizer memory.
Audit supervised token masks, templates, and dataset splits.
Evaluate adapters and choose a compatible deployment format.

sections.title: 1. Identify the failure before choosing fine-tuning
paragraphs: Fine-tuning means taking a pretrained language model (the kind behind assistants like ChatGPT or Claude) and continuing to train it on your own examples, so its weights shift toward the behavior you want. Put another way, it changes the model's learned response distribution. Most of this article is about doing that cheaply with LoRA and QLoRA, but before reaching for any training at all, it's worth pinning down what problem you're solving. Fine-tuning is useful when a stable task requires behavior that prompting does not reliably elicit: consistent domain terminology, a specialized extraction convention, or a repeated decision pattern supported by many trustworthy examples. The first engineering question is therefore what fails, under which inputs, and how success will be scored. A few attractive demonstrations are insufficient evidence that the behavior generalizes.

Begin with a prompt baseline, including representative demonstrations when context permits. If failures arise because the model lacks current policies or customer-specific records, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG, which looks up relevant documents and pastes them into the prompt; see the RAG: Retrieving Evidence Before Generating Answers article) supplies those records at request time. Fine-tuning is a poor replacement for a frequently changing database: updating weights complicates freshness, attribution, and deletion. Retrieval and adaptation can cooperate, though. An adapter (a small set of extra trainable weights attached to a frozen model, which we'll build up in section 3) can teach how to use retrieved evidence while the index remains responsible for supplying the evidence.

A useful design exercise is to label a sample of failures as missing evidence, instruction ambiguity, output-contract violation, or reasoning error. Fix evidence and instructions first, then estimate the remaining addressable error. For strict JSON output, a constrained decoder (a generation mode that only allows tokens that keep the output valid against a schema) may remove syntax failures without training. For incorrect field meanings, examples and training may help. This decomposition gives you a defensible investment decision and sets the baselines an adapter has to beat to justify its operational complexity. The figure at the end of this section lines up the three main options (prompting and decoding, retrieval, and fine-tuning) by the kind of failure each one addresses.

sections.title: 2. SFT describes the objective; LoRA describes what changes
paragraphs: Once you've decided training is worth it, two separate questions come up: what is the model being trained toward, and which weights are allowed to change? It helps to keep those apart. Supervised fine-tuning, or SFT, answers the first one. It usually minimizes next-token negative log likelihood on desired responses conditioned on their prompts, which in plain terms means penalizing the model whenever it assigns low probability to the correct next token of a good answer. Full fine-tuning and LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation, derived in section 3) can optimize exactly this same objective. They differ in the trainable parameterization, which answers the second question. Full fine-tuning updates the original weights; parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) freezes most original parameters and learns a smaller set. Calling SFT and LoRA competing objectives confuses the training signal with the mechanism that receives its gradients.

Full fine-tuning offers unrestricted updates to the selected model parameters, but requires larger optimizer state (the extra values an optimizer like Adam tracks for every trainable weight, counted in section 5) and produces a complete task-specific checkpoint. LoRA constrains each selected matrix update to a low-rank factorization, allowing compact task artifacts. QLoRA (quantized LoRA, covered in section 4) additionally compresses the frozen backbone, meaning the large pretrained model underneath the adapter. Neither method guarantees the quality of full fine-tuning on an arbitrary distribution. A narrow output convention and a substantial language-domain shift can require different adaptation capacity, coverage, and datasets.

So how do you pick between them? In an interview, justify the smallest experiment that resolves uncertainty. Hold the base revision, data split, evaluation prompts, and token budget fixed. Compare the prompt baseline with a modest adapter before committing to a larger training run. Escalate target coverage, rank, or full fine-tuning when evidence indicates insufficient capacity (target coverage and rank, roughly which matrices get an adapter and how expressive each adapter is, are explained in the next section). If training error is already low but held-out performance is poor, more trainable parameters are unlikely to repair a sampling or labeling problem.

sections.title: 3. Derive the adapter instead of memorizing its name
paragraphs: Let's start with the algebra, since LoRA is simpler than its name suggests. Much of a transformer's work happens in linear projections: weight matrices that turn one vector into another (the attention and feed-forward layers from the Inside a decoder: from text to the next token article are built from them). For a linear projection W₀ with d_out rows and d_in columns, LoRA adds B A, where A maps the input into r coordinates and B maps those coordinates to the output. The original matrix stays frozen. The number r is the rank: roughly, how many independent directions the update can push the output in. A rough analogy is a mixing board where, instead of touching every channel's slider, you get a handful of master knobs that each move many sliders together in a fixed pattern. Note that the rank bound applies to the update, not to W₀ or the resulting model. Standard LoRA also scales the update by α/r, where alpha (α) is a number you choose. Rank controls representational capacity; alpha controls the scale of the learned branch. Their effects interact with initialization and optimization, so changing rank is not a clean capacity experiment unless scaling is considered. The walkthrough below makes this concrete with a toy 2×2 matrix at rank 1: the thin factors B (a column) and A (a row) multiply into a full-size but rank-one update, that update is added to the frozen W, and then one input follows both branches to the same output.

The toy example doesn't save anything, but real sizes do. Take a square 4,096-by-4,096 projection and rank 16. The original matrix has 16,777,216 parameters. Its two factors contain 16 × (4,096 + 4,096) = 131,072 trainable parameters, or 0.78125% of the original count. At alpha 32, the multiplier is 2. If two such projections are adapted in each of 32 layers, the total is 8,388,608 parameters. This is a deliberately simplified architecture calculation, not a count for every model: grouped-query attention (where several query heads share one key/value head, covered in the Efficient Attention: Heads, Memory Traffic, and Context article) can make key and value projections rectangular.

Which matrices get an adapter, often called the target modules, is a separate capacity decision. Adapting only query and value projections costs less than covering attention and feed-forward projections, but may leave important transformations fixed. Inspect actual module names and tensor shapes instead of copying a configuration from another architecture. Common initialization makes one factor zero and the other random, preserving the base behavior initially; setting both to zero would prevent useful initial gradients through their product. (The walkthrough above uses nonzero factors on purpose, to show what a trained update looks like.) Hugging Face's PEFT library also supports variants with different scaling, so record the variant alongside rank and alpha. The figure at the end of this section recaps the whole computation: one input feeding a frozen path and a trainable path, summed at the output.
sections.formula: h = W₀x + (α/r)B(Ax); A ∈ ℝ^(r×d_in), B ∈ ℝ^(d_out×r); N_adapter = r(d_in + d_out); rank(BA) ≤ r

sections.title: 4. QLoRA separates weight storage from arithmetic
paragraphs: LoRA shrinks what you train, but the frozen backbone still has to sit in GPU memory, and for a large model that's often the biggest single cost. QLoRA goes after that part. It stores the frozen backbone in a low-bit representation (quantization: keeping each weight as a small integer code plus a shared scale, rather than a 16-bit number; the Quantization and Compression: Spend Fewer Bits Without Losing the Task article goes deeper) while training higher-precision LoRA factors. Think of it like keeping a library of books zipped on disk and unzipping just the chapter you need when you read it. The original method combines four-bit NormalFloat (NF4), quantization of quantization constants, and paged optimizers. NF4 allocates representable values for a normal-distribution assumption, since trained weights tend to cluster around zero in a roughly bell-shaped way; it is not simply a uniformly spaced signed integer format. Double quantization compresses the per-block scales themselves, reducing metadata overhead. Paged optimizers let optimizer state spill to CPU memory during spikes instead of triggering an out-of-memory error. These choices address different memory terms rather than multiplying into a universal speedup. The walkthrough below shows the core idea on a schematic weight block: the frozen weights live as 4-bit codes plus a scale, get decoded to BF16 (a 16-bit floating-point format common in training) for the actual math, and sit beside BF16 adapter factors A and B that remain trainable.

The key distinction here is storage precision versus compute precision. Quantized weight blocks are dequantized as needed for arithmetic, commonly using BF16, while the adapter stays trainable. Backpropagation must still transmit gradients through computations involving frozen weights so that earlier adapters receive a learning signal. Frozen does not mean absent from the forward or backward graph. It means that the backbone does not accumulate trainable weight updates and optimizer state. That's the last step of the walkthrough above: gradients pass through both branches, but only A and B change.

In practice, a few things can go wrong quietly. A practical implementation must prepare the quantized model for training and verify that only intended parameters require gradients. Quantization support depends on the backend and model architecture; a four-bit inference loader alone is not a complete training recipe. Before the expensive run, inspect trainable names, perform a short forward/backward pass, and confirm that adapter gradients are finite and that the loss changes. Keep the compute dtype, quantization settings, and preparation code in the experiment manifest. The figure at the end of this section summarizes where each precision boundary sits, from compressed storage through the backward pass.

sections.title: 5. Count optimizer state, then account for the missing memory
paragraphs: With the backbone compressed, the natural next question is whether the whole training run fits on your GPU. Parameter count alone is not a training memory estimate. Separate persistent weights, gradients, optimizer moments, optional master copies, activations, temporary workspaces, and allocator overhead. Adam-like optimization commonly maintains two moment tensors per trainable parameter: a running average of each weight's gradient and a running average of its squared gradient. Their precision matters. A frozen weight needs storage but no optimizer moments, which is why a small adapter can reduce training memory substantially even when its backbone remains in a conventional precision.

Using the 8,388,608-parameter adapter above, assume BF16 weights and gradients at two bytes each, FP32 first and second moments at four bytes each, and an FP32 master copy at four bytes (a higher-precision copy of the weights that the optimizer updates, so tiny updates don't get rounded away). The total is 16 bytes per trainable parameter, or 128 MiB. Without that master copy, it is 96 MiB. The bar chart at the end of this section breaks those totals into their components. These are explicit accounting scenarios, not universal framework behavior. An ideal four-bit payload for a seven-billion-parameter backbone is 3.5 billion bytes before scales, unquantized tensors, and runtime overhead.

The adapter's tensors are the easy part to count. Activations (the intermediate values saved during the forward pass so the backward pass can compute gradients) still depend on sequence length, microbatch size, architecture, and checkpointing. Gradient accumulation (summing gradients over several small microbatches before one optimizer step) increases the effective batch without retaining all microbatches' activations simultaneously. Activation checkpointing trades recomputation for memory: it throws away some activations and recomputes them during the backward pass. Paging can absorb optimizer-state pressure but may incur transfers; it does not eliminate the underlying storage requirement. Measure peak allocated and reserved memory on representative long examples, because a successful short smoke test does not demonstrate that the production training distribution fits.
sections.formula: M_train ≈ M_frozen + N_trainable(b_weights + b_gradients + b_moments + b_master) + M_activations + M_workspace; 1 MiB = 2²⁰ bytes

sections.title: 6. The dataset includes the template and loss mask
paragraphs: So far we've focused on the model side. The data side is where a lot of quiet bugs tend to hide, because an SFT example is more than a prompt-response pair stored in JSON. Role delimiters, special tokens, assistant boundaries, end-of-turn markers, and token masks determine the actual objective. Use the model's intended chat template (the model-specific format that wraps each message in role markers and special tokens) consistently at training and serving time. Do not add a generation prompt blindly during training, or duplicate special tokens when a formatted string is tokenized again. Decode several tokenized examples and inspect the exact boundary where the assistant response starts.

Once the text is formatted, the next question is which tokens the model actually learns from. Assistant-only supervision usually excludes user, system, and padding tokens from the loss while retaining them as conditioning context. A label mask is different from an attention mask: excluding a token as a prediction target does not necessarily hide it from attention. It's a bit like a student reading the whole exam question but only being graded on their answer. The formula below writes this out: each position t gets a mask value m_t of 1 (graded) or 0 (context only), and the loss averages over the graded positions. Hugging Face's TRL library has an assistant-only mode that requires template support for identifying assistant spans. Explicitly inspect which token positions contribute to loss, including tool conversations and truncated samples. An example whose answer is entirely truncated can contain zero useful supervised targets.

Finally, how you split the data matters as much as how you format it. Split before deriving variants such as paraphrases or augmentations. Keep the same customer, source document, conversation family, or synthetic seed on one side of the boundary when those relationships create leakage (near-identical information landing in both training and test data, which inflates test scores). Prefer a time-based test when future traffic is the intended use case. Deduplicate near-copies across splits and retain rare failure categories. Training on many paraphrases of a single answer can make token counts look impressive while adding little independent evidence. A reviewed dataset manifest should document provenance, labeling rules, exclusions, and split membership. The figure at the end of this section puts these checks in order, from grouping and splitting through the truncation check.
sections.formula: L = −[Σ_t m_t log pθ(y_t | tokens before t)] / [Σ_t m_t]; m_t ∈ {0,1}; require Σ_t m_t > 0

sections.title: 7. Evaluate the behavior and the system separately
paragraphs: Once an adapter is trained, you need evidence that it actually helped. Validation loss detects some training problems but cannot establish product success. For extraction, measure schema validity, field-level precision and recall, and unsupported values separately. For evidence-grounded answering, score answer correctness and evidence support. Include abstention cases, conflicting documents, long inputs, and out-of-domain requests. Compare against the same base model with the best established prompt, then examine regressions in general instruction following and safety-sensitive behaviors relevant to the application.

The process around those metrics matters too. Choose checkpoints and hyperparameters on development data, then evaluate the selected recipe once on a protected test set. Report uncertainty and inspect failures rather than promoting small score differences automatically. Fix decoding settings and template versions for comparisons. Separately measure peak memory, training tokens per second, serving latency, and adapter-loading overhead on the intended hardware. An adapter that improves average correctness but worsens rare high-cost errors may need better examples or an explicit routing policy before deployment.

sections.title: 8. Deploy a reproducible base-and-adapter contract
paragraphs: The last step is getting the adapter into production, and here it helps to remember what an adapter actually is: a small patch on top of a specific base model. An adapter checkpoint is not normally a standalone model. Deploy it with the exact compatible base revision, tokenizer, chat template, target-module configuration, and relevant quantization settings. Keeping adapters separate enables one resident backbone to serve multiple specialized behaviors, provided the serving engine supports the ranks and modules used. Benchmark realistic adapter mixtures: loading, eviction, and batching behavior can dominate the modest arithmetic added by a low-rank branch.

The alternative is to bake the adapter into the base weights. For ordinary floating-point LoRA, a merged weight is W₀ + (α/r)BA, the same addition you saw in the section 3 walkthrough. This removes the separate adapter branch but creates a full model artifact. PEFT's merge-and-unload path discards adapter-management capabilities in the returned model, and some quantization configurations do not support merging. Preserve the original adapter and base references for rollback. Merging several task updates also does not guarantee that their behaviors compose without interference.

Quantized deployment adds another boundary: merging into a higher-precision backbone and then requantizing changes numerical error relative to the training computation. Do not assume equivalent outputs simply because the algebra matches in real arithmetic. Validate the actual exported artifact, including representative long prompts and rare categories, before a staged release. Record checksums and evaluation results together so a rollback restores the complete serving configuration rather than only a filename. The figure at the end of this section compares the two deployment contracts, a separate adapter versus a merged model, side by side.

interview.question: A support team has 30,000 reviewed ticket-to-JSON examples, weekly policy changes, and a limited GPU budget. The base model produces valid JSON but often uses the wrong escalation category. Propose an adaptation and release plan.
interview.answer: First separate policy-evidence failures from stable category-mapping errors. Retrieve current policy and establish a prompt baseline; train a modest LoRA or QLoRA adapter only for the remaining behavioral gap. Group tickets by customer and conversation before splitting, use a future-time holdout, and inspect assistant loss masks and truncation. Budget backbone storage, adapter optimizer state, and long-sequence activations explicitly. Select rank and target modules on development results, measuring category precision/recall and costly escalation mistakes rather than JSON validity alone. Compare with the unchanged baseline and test general behavior regressions. Deploy the exact base-adapter-template combination through a staged rollout, validate any merged or requantized artifact independently, and retain a complete rollback configuration. Weekly policy updates remain in retrieval unless the stable task definition itself changes.

pitfalls: Treating SFT and LoRA as mutually exclusive training objectives.
Reporting a parameter reduction as the same reduction in total GPU memory or FLOPs.
Assuming four-bit weight storage means every operation and gradient uses four bits.
Copying target-module names without inspecting the actual architecture.
Splitting paraphrases or related conversations across training and test sets.
Masking attention when the intention was only to exclude prompt tokens from loss.
Deploying an adapter on an unpinned base revision or different chat template.
Assuming merged and requantized artifacts preserve the evaluated behavior automatically.
checklist: Classify baseline failures and choose measurable acceptance criteria.
Pin base revision, tokenizer, template, quantization backend, and training libraries.
Record independent split groups and review labels for rare costly cases.
Inspect decoded token sequences, masks, truncation, and trainable tensor names.
Calculate parameter and optimizer-state counts; measure representative peak memory.
Compare target coverage, rank, and scaling with a controlled development budget.
Evaluate task quality, regressions, and intended serving performance separately.
Validate the final export and preserve the complete rollback manifest.

flashcards.front: When is retrieval preferable to fine-tuning?
flashcards.back: When the failure is missing or changing evidence. Retrieval supplies current attributable facts at request time, while weight updates make freshness and provenance harder to manage.

flashcards.front: Why can training be both SFT and LoRA?
flashcards.back: SFT specifies supervised response-token prediction; LoRA specifies the trainable parameterization. The same supervised loss can update all original weights or only adapter factors.

flashcards.front: What is low rank in LoRA?
flashcards.back: The matrix update BA has rank at most r. The frozen base matrix and the final effective matrix need not be low rank.

flashcards.front: How many trainable parameters adapt a d_out-by-d_in matrix at rank r?
flashcards.back: r(d_in + d_out), excluding biases or other trainable modules, because A has r × d_in entries and B has d_out × r entries.

flashcards.front: How many parameters does rank-16 LoRA add to a 4096-by-4096 projection?
flashcards.back: 131,072, or 0.78125% of the original 16,777,216 parameters. This is a parameter ratio, not a total training-memory ratio.

flashcards.front: How do rank and alpha differ?
flashcards.back: Rank limits update capacity; alpha sets branch scaling through alpha/r in standard LoRA. Changing rank also changes scaling unless alpha or the scaling convention is adjusted.

flashcards.front: Why not initialize both LoRA factors to zero?
flashcards.back: Both factor gradients would initially vanish through the product. One zero factor and one random factor preserve the initial base output while allowing learning to begin.

flashcards.front: Does QLoRA compute everything in four bits?
flashcards.back: No. Its frozen backbone uses low-bit storage, while dequantized arithmetic and trainable adapter tensors use supported higher precision. Storage dtype and compute dtype are distinct.

flashcards.front: Why does a frozen backbone still participate in backpropagation?
flashcards.back: Gradients must flow through its computations to reach trainable adapters in earlier layers. Freezing removes backbone parameter updates and optimizer state, not the dependency graph.

flashcards.front: Why is adapter parameter count insufficient to predict GPU memory?
flashcards.back: Memory also includes backbone storage, gradients, optimizer moments, possible master weights, activations, and workspaces. Sequence length can make activations dominate despite a tiny adapter.

flashcards.front: How does a loss mask differ from an attention mask?
flashcards.back: A loss mask excludes positions as supervised targets; an attention mask governs which positions can be attended to. Prompt tokens may remain necessary context even when excluded from loss.

flashcards.front: Why split before creating paraphrased training variants?
flashcards.back: Otherwise related variants can appear in both training and evaluation, rewarding memorization of the same underlying case rather than generalization to independent cases.

flashcards.front: Why does lower validation loss not prove a better product?
flashcards.back: Token likelihood can improve while costly category mistakes, unsupported claims, or long-input failures worsen. Task metrics and regression slices must test the actual acceptance criteria.

flashcards.front: What must be checked before deploying a merged QLoRA result?
flashcards.back: Verify backend merge support, exact base compatibility, tokenizer and template versions, and the exported artifact's quality. Dequantization and requantization alter numerical error, so algebraic equivalence does not guarantee equivalent behavior.
